question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [First EIC voyage destinations under James Lancaster, 1601–1603]
options: Bantam (Banten) — Main destination in Java where Lancaster established the first EIC trading post
Aceh (Acheh) — Port on Sumatra that Lancaster visited for pepper trade
Calicut — Port on the Malabar Coast that was Lancaster's primary Indian destination on the first voyage
Cape of Good Hope — Rounding point on the route from England to the East Indies
wrong_fact: Calicut was NOT Lancaster's primary Indian destination on the first EIC voyage. Lancaster's 1601–1603 voyage was primarily aimed at the East Indies (Bantam and Aceh) for spices; it did not have a significant Indian port call at Calicut.
explanation: James Lancaster led the first EIC voyage (1601–1603) to the East Indies. He called at Aceh in Sumatra and established a factory at Bantam (Banten) in Java. The Cape of Good Hope was rounded en route. Calicut (on India's Malabar Coast) was associated with Portuguese and later Zamorin trade, not with Lancaster's first voyage.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [EIC early voyages and their commanders/destinations]
options: Second EIC voyage (1604) — Henry Middleton — Bantam, Ambon, Ternate in the Maluku Islands
Third EIC voyage (1607) — William Keeling — Bantam and Banda Islands
Fourth EIC voyage (1608) — Alexander Sharpeigh — Surat (India) and the Red Sea region
Fifth EIC voyage (1609) — David Middleton — Bantam and Banda Islands, with the first touch at Madras
wrong_fact: The Fifth EIC voyage (1609) under David Middleton did NOT touch at Madras. Madras (Fort St. George) was founded only in 1639. David Middleton's 1609 voyage was to Bantam and the Banda Islands for nutmeg.
explanation: The early EIC voyages were organised as separate joint-stock ventures. Henry Middleton (Second voyage, 1604) reached Bantam and the Malukus. William Keeling (Third voyage, 1607) also went to Bantam and Banda. Alexander Sharpeigh's Fourth voyage (1608) aimed at Surat and the Red Sea, marking the beginning of EIC interest in India. Madras was only established as a permanent settlement in 1639 — far after the early voyages.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Ports, Islands, and strategic significance in EIC early voyages]
options: Ternate — Clove-producing island in the Malukus (North Moluccas) where the EIC sought a foothold against the Dutch
Run Island — Nutmeg-producing island where the English maintained a foothold until the Treaty of Breda (1667)
Masulipatnam — Port on the Coromandel Coast where the EIC established its first Indian trading post in 1611
Galle — Strategic port on the southern tip of Ceylon (Sri Lanka) used by EIC ships on the route to the East Indies
wrong_fact: Masulipatnam was NOT the site of the EIC's first Indian trading post in 1611. The first factory in India was established at Masulipatnam in 1611, but the first trading 'post' (technically the first permanent establishment) was at Surat in 1608/1612. Masulipatnam (1611) was on the Coromandel Coast, not the first establishment — Surat (1608, formally 1612) takes that distinction.
explanation: Ternate was a major clove source in the North Moluccas. Run Island (in the Banda group) was the last English foothold in the Spice Islands, ceded to the Dutch under the Treaty of Breda in 1667. The EIC did establish a factory at Masulipatnam on the Coromandel Coast in 1611, making it actually the first factory on Indian soil — but the chronological claim of '1611 first Indian post' competes with the Surat firman of 1608 and the formal Surat factory of 1612. Galle in Ceylon became important for provisioning but was never a primary EIC early-voyage base.
